Section 84 of the Penal Code reads : Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law." This section shows that an act of a person of unsound mind, who at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of his mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, is .not an offence. There is no doubt that the burden to prove insanity lies upon the defence. 

 23. Section 84 contains in Chapter IV of the Penal Code under the heading "General Exception". In this chapter there are 30 sections from section 76- 106. It is apparent from the exceptions mentioned above that the test of criminality in the Penal Code depends upon the presence of criminal intent. It is the keynote of this chapter as it is of the English Criminal Law that in order to hold a person guilty of an offence, the existence of mens rea in him is fundamental when the accused relies on a general exception contained in Chapter IV of the Penal Code, in view of section 105 of the Evidence Act the Court is bound to presume the absence of circumstances, which bring the case of the accused within that exception, and consequently, the burden for proving the exception is on the accused. Section 105 of the Evidence Act reads: 

 "105. Burden of proving the case of accused comes within exceptions. When a person is accused of any offence, the burden for proving the existence of circumstances bringing the case within any of the General Exceptions in the Penal Code, or within any special exception or proviso contained in any other part of the same Code, or in any law defining the offence, is upon him, and the Court shall presume the absence of such circumstances". 

 24. In that case it was also observed that even if the accused was not able to establish conclusively that he was insane at the time he committed the offence, the evidence placed by the prosecution may raise a reasonable doubt in the mind of the court as regards one or more of the ingredients of the offence, including mens rea of the accused and in that case, the court would be entitled to give benefit to the accused on the ground that the general burden of proof resting on the prosecution was not discharged. On an analysis of the evidence on record we found that the condemned-prisoner was completely insane at or about the time of occurrence has been admitted by the prosecution witnesses. In case where accused set up a plea of insanity and establishes his plea the Court is burdened with the matter to look into it carefully. Under such circumstances the onus of the prosecution is not merely to establish that the accused has committed the criminal act, but also to establish that he has the necessary mens rea, which is also an ingredient of the offence.
